## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

{{< include ../learning_objectives/0310-github-pull-requests.qmd >}}

## Creating a pull request

To create a pull request, you first need
to ensure all the local changes you made on the new branch are also available on the remote repository (i.e., you need to push them).
Once that has happened, you need to go to the remote GitHub repository,
as pull requests are created from there.

GitHub often tries to be helpful when a change is pushed to a new branch
that doesn't yet exist on the default branch by showing you a yellow banner listing any recently pushed branches.

<img src="../img/create-pr.png" width="100%">

To create a pull request, you click the green button "Compare & pull request".
In the new page, add a message to describe the changes you have made, scroll down to review the changed files,
and then click the green button that reads "Create pull request".
If you are working together in a team, you could also designate certain team members to review your work
and assign relevant labels, via the right-hand side panel.

The next step is for a collaborator to review your work and merge it in if they approve it (see [Code review on GitHub](0320-github-code-review.qmd)).

:::{.exercise}

1. Use the green "Compare & pull request" button on the yellow banner to open a pull request.

2. Go to the "Pull requests" tab on the remote GitHub repository and explore the "Conversation"
   and "Files changed" sub-tabs there.
:::

## Draft pull requests

Sometimes you want to open a pull request before the work is finished, to show your teammates
where you are heading, to ask for early feedback,
or to see whether your changes pass the project's automated checks.
Instead of adding "WIP" (work in progress) to the title, open the pull request as a **draft**.
On the page where you write the pull request's description, use the drop-down arrow beside the green "Create pull request" button,
select "Create draft pull request",
and then click "Draft pull request".

A draft pull request cannot be merged,
and it tells your teammates that it is not ready for review yet.
When the work is ready, click "Ready for review" in the merge box at the bottom of the pull request's "Conversation" tab.
If you need to go back to working on it, click "Convert to draft" under "Reviewers" in the right-hand sidebar.

## How do you not accept a pull request?

In some cases, it might not make sense to merge a pull request.
To close a pull request that should not be merged, scroll to the bottom of the pull request page,
and look for a gray "Closes pull request" button.
This will move the pull request to the closed pull requests section (similar to closed issues)
and does not merge the changes.

<img src="../img/close-pr.png" width="100%">
